extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers interested in narratology and narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: An outline of Gérard Genette's core narratological concepts used to analyse and describe narrative discourse (order, frequency, duration, voice, mood) plus related textual concepts such as paratext and hypotext. Useful for applying Genette's terminology to creative-writing analysis or critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order (anachrony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts for the relation between chronological order of events and the order in which they are presented in the narrative; disarrangements on the level of order are termed 'anachrony'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If events chronologically are B1, A2, C3 but arranged in the text as A2 (discovery), B1 (flashback), C3 (resolution), the reader recognises effects such as flashback. This concept covers flashback, flash-forward, simultaneity and rarer effects produced by non-chronological presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between how often an event occurs and how often it is narrated: singular, iterative, repetitive, or multiple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and examples from the page: singular — an event occurs once and is narrated once ('Today I went to the shop'); iterative — occurs many times but narrated once ('I used to go to the shop'); repetitive — occurs once but narrated many times ('Today I went to the shop' + 'Today he went to the shop'); multiple — occurs many times and narrated many times ('I used to go to the shop' + 'He used to go to the shop' + 'I went to the shop yesterday'). Use this to describe narrative strategies that compress, expand, or multiply events in telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration (discourse time vs narrative time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes discourse time (time taken by the telling) from narrative time (time covered by the events); these two elements form duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: 'Five years passed' — long narrative time (five years) but short discourse time (a second to read). James Joyce's Ulysses: short narrative time (24 hours) but long discourse time (takes long to read). Use this to analyse pacing, stretching or compression of time, and the narrative effect of temporal manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice (diegesis and narratorial position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns who narrates and from where; categorises narration by diegetic level and whether the narrator is a character in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two axes given: where is the narration from — intra-diegetic (inside the text) versus extra-diegetic (outside the text); is the narrator a character — hetero-diegetic (not a character) versus homo-diegetic (a character). Examples: intra-diegetic — Wilkie Collins' The Woman in White; extra-diegetic — Thomas Hardy's Tess of the D'Urbervilles; hetero-diegetic — Homer's The Odyssey; homo-diegetic — Wuthering Heights. Use these labels to specify narratorial emplacement and its effect on authority, knowledge, and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mood (distance and perspective; reported/transposed/narrated speech; focalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative mood depends on the narrator's 'distance' and 'perspective' and is linked to voice; involves how characters' speech and consciousness are represented and the focalization of perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance changes with: narrated speech (words/actions integrated into narration), transposed speech (indirect style or free indirect style — indirect reports character's words via narrator's interpretation; free indirect reports without subordinate conjunction), and reported speech (character's words cited verbatim). Perspective is termed focalization: narratives can be non-focalized, internally focalized, or externally focalized. Use these distinctions to analyse the closeness of narration to character consciousness, modes of speech representation, and shifts in viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paratext
rubrics_metrics.description: The material accompanying the text — prefaces, introductions, illustrations or other material — which Genette terms 'paratext'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paratexts function as 'thresholds of interpretation' that frame reading and meaning (see Paratexts: Thresholds of Interpretation). Consider how titles, prefaces, dedications, illustrations and publisher apparatus shape reception and interpretation of the main text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotext
rubrics_metrics.description: The source texts or prior texts from which a given text derives; Genette uses the term 'hypotext' for these sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotext indicates relationships such as adaptation, transformation, parody, or rewriting; identifying hypotexts helps analyse intertextual relations and 'literature in the second degree' (palimpsest/transformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhetorical vocabulary (trope and metonymy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genette reintroduced rhetorical vocabulary into literary criticism, for example terms such as 'trope' and 'metonymy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying rhetorical terms helps diagnose figurative operations within narrative and discourse. Although briefly mentioned, this signals a criterion: attend to tropes and figures (metonymy, etc.) when analysing rhetorical and figurative dimensions of texts.
